ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is a capacitive pressure sensor; the upper part is a fixed electrode, and the lower part is a movable diaphragm electrode; the arrow of force F points upward, indicating that F presses the diaphragm electrode upward, making the distance between the two plates decrease. The upper plate is connected through the upper resistor R to point b of the vertical branch on the right side, and then through the galvanometer G to point a. In the lower power supply symbol, the long plate on the left side is the positive electrode, and the short plate on the right side is the negative electrode; the positive electrode is connected to the movable diaphragm electrode, and the negative electrode is connected to point a. Reasoning: When F presses the diaphragm upward, the distance d between the two plates of the capacitor decreases, and from C=εS/d it can be known that the capacitance C increases. The power supply voltage U remains unchanged, so from Q=CU it can be known that the capacitor needs to be further charged, and the amount of charge carried by the plates increases. Since the movable diaphragm electrode is connected to the positive electrode of the power supply, it should increase positive charge; the upper plate correspondingly increases negative charge. Conventional current in the external circuit goes from the upper plate through R to point b, then through the galvanometer G to point a, with direction b→a. Therefore, saying “If F presses the diaphragm electrode upward, there is a current in the circuit from a to b” is opposite to the actual instantaneous current direction, and is an incorrect statement.
